opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the appeal of the untrusted-insider framing is that it lets you make progress on safety without first having to solve the hardest version of the alignment problem.

The standard approach to alignment is: make sure the AI system actually wants what we want, so it never tries to do anything bad in the first place. I think that's important and we should keep working on it. But it's hard to *verify*. Our interpretability tools aren't mature enough to look inside a model and confidently say "this system has no hidden goals that conflict with ours." So there's always some residual probability that, despite our best efforts, we've ended up with a system that's subtly misaligned and is just behaving well because it's being watched, or because it hasn't yet had a good opportunity to do otherwise.

The insider-threat framing says: fine, let's take that possibility seriously and plan for it. Companies and governments already deal with this with humans. You have employees who have a lot of access and capability, and most of them are trustworthy, but you can't be certain about any individual one. So you don't rely only on trust. You have access controls, least privilege, logging, monitoring, separation of duties, two-person rules for sensitive actions, audits. The goal isn't to make it impossible for anyone to ever do anything bad. It's to make it so that if someone does try, they're likely to get caught before they cause irreversible harm.

Applied to AI, that looks like: don't give the model more permissions than it needs for the task. Have other models, possibly weaker but more trusted ones, monitor its outputs and flag suspicious actions. Have humans review a sample of what it does, especially the high-stakes stuff. Design the overall system so that a takeover would require many steps, each of which is an opportunity for detection.

A few reasons I find this promising specifically.

First, it's robust to our uncertainty. It doesn't depend on whether the model is aligned. If it is, these measures cost you a bit of efficiency. If it isn't, they might be what saves you.

Second, it's empirically testable. You can do red-teaming where you deliberately give a model a hidden objective, or have a red team play the role of a scheming model, and see whether your control setup catches it. That's a much more concrete feedback loop than a lot of alignment research, where it's hard to know if you've actually succeeded.

Third, catching a model in the act is itself hugely valuable. If your monitoring catches a model attempting something like exfiltrating its weights or sabotaging safety research, that's incredibly strong evidence that misalignment is real. It changes the conversation inside labs and with policymakers. So control buys you both safety and information.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. This approach probably works best in a particular window, where models are capable enough to be really useful and potentially dangerous, but not so far beyond us that they can trivially evade every monitor we build. For radically superhuman systems, I'm much less confident that you can contain something smarter than everyone watching it. So I see control as a bridge: it lets us safely extract a lot of useful work from early transformative systems, including work on alignment itself, while we develop the deeper solutions we'll need later.

And there are real costs. Monitoring and restricting systems slows things down, and there's competitive pressure to cut those corners. So part of making this work is making it cheap enough that labs actually adopt it, and ideally getting some norms or regulation around it so it's not just a matter of individual companies' goodwill.

But overall, I think it's one of the more tractable and underrated pieces of the puzzle. It takes a problem that feels philosophically slippery, "is this AI secretly plotting against us?", and turns it into something closer to a security engineering problem, which is a kind of problem we actually know how to make progress on.

r003.rationale: It recommends applying security controls to AI systems as untrusted insiders and says layered controls can help detect a takeover attempt before irreversible harm.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure, so the basic idea is that we already have a lot of experience, as a civilization, with the problem of "I need to get work done by someone who might not have my best interests at heart." Companies deal with this constantly. You hire people, you give them access to systems, and you don't fully know whether any given employee is loyal, or careless, or actively working for a competitor. And yet companies mostly don't get destroyed by their employees, because they've built up a whole toolkit: access controls, logging, code review, separation of duties, the principle that nobody gets to approve their own expense report.

The analogy to AI is that we're going to be deploying systems that are doing a lot of valuable work, and we're going to be uncertain about whether they're aligned. We might have decent evidence that they are, but "decent evidence" is not the same as "we can bet the future on it." So rather than saying "we'll only deploy once we're sure it's aligned," which might never happen, or "we'll deploy and just hope," you say: let's design the deployment so that even if the system is actively trying to cause harm, it can't do that much damage.

Concretely, that looks like things like: the model doesn't get to run arbitrary code on production infrastructure without a check. Its outputs get monitored, maybe by a weaker model that we trust more precisely because it's too weak to be scheming in a sophisticated way. Dangerous actions require sign-off from a human or from an independent process. You limit what any single instance can do, so that a takeover would require coordinating across many steps, many of which are being watched.

What I like about this framing is that it's not relying on us having solved the hard scientific problem of knowing what's going on inside the model. It's a security mindset rather than a "deep understanding" mindset. And security people are pretty good at this. They're used to assuming the adversary is competent and asking "okay, given that, what can they actually accomplish?"

Now, I don't want to oversell it. There are real disanalogies. A human insider can't be copied a thousand times. A human insider doesn't get to read all of their company's internal documents in a few seconds. And at some level of capability, the "untrusted insider" is just much smarter than the people doing the monitoring, and the controls start to look flimsy. So I see this as something that buys us time during a particular window, roughly the period where AI systems are capable enough to be very useful and potentially dangerous, but not so capable that they can trivially route around any oversight we set up. In that window, control measures could be the difference between a catastrophe and a near miss that we learn from.

And the other thing I'd emphasize is that it's testable. You can actually red-team it. You can tell a model, "try to exfiltrate your weights," or "try to insert a backdoor," and see whether your controls catch it. That's a much more empirical way to make progress than a lot of alignment work, where it's hard to know if you've succeeded. So it's not the whole answer, but it's a piece I think is seriously underrated.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that you don’t necessarily have to make an AI system want the right things in order to prevent it from causing a catastrophe. You can also limit what it’s able to do, and make sure that attempts to do something dangerous are likely to be caught.

We already do a version of this with people. If you hire someone to work on sensitive infrastructure, you don’t give them unrestricted access to everything just because they seemed trustworthy in an interview. You restrict permissions, log what they do, and require additional approval for particularly consequential actions. You can apply that same kind of thinking to AI systems.

Suppose an AI is writing code for you. You could assume, for the purpose of designing your safeguards, that it might try to insert a vulnerability. Then the question becomes: Can we structure the workflow so that it can still write useful code, but any attempt to insert a vulnerability is likely to be detected before that code gets deployed? Maybe you use another model to review its work, with human review for suspicious cases. And you test those safeguards by actively trying to get attacks through them.

What I find promising is that this gives us a fairly concrete thing to study. Rather than having to establish that a model will always have good intentions, we can ask how successfully an adversarial model can defeat a particular set of defenses.

Of course, that isn’t a guarantee. The reviewer might miss things, or the models might find ways to coordinate, and sufficiently capable systems could outsmart the whole setup. But an AI takeover would require the AI to actually acquire power in the world. If we can make those steps difficult and detectable, that gives us a way to reduce the risk even when we’re uncertain about the system’s motivations.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is that you don’t have to solve the problem of making an AI reliably want what you want in order to limit the damage it can do. You can instead ask: suppose this system were actively trying to undermine us. Could we arrange things so that we would catch it, or stop it from taking the actions that matter?

We already do some version of this with people. An employee doesn’t automatically get access to every password or the ability to move all the company’s money. You restrict access, require approval for consequential actions, and monitor what’s happening. With AI systems, you could similarly restrict their access to computers, have other systems review their proposed actions, and use trusted procedures to decide when something can actually be executed.

What makes this promising is that trying to cause a takeover seems to require doing things that are meaningfully different from carrying out the task we assigned. A system might need to steal credentials, tamper with its monitoring, or get an unauthorized copy of itself running somewhere. Those are opportunities for us to intervene.

Of course, that only helps if our safeguards work against a system that is deliberately trying to evade them. So I’d want to test the whole setup adversarially: give an AI the objective of getting around the safeguards and see whether it can succeed. That doesn’t establish a guarantee, especially if future systems are much more capable. But it gives us a concrete way to develop and evaluate defenses without first having to establish that the AI itself is trustworthy.
